newsitem.title: USA: IMF warns of risks in Europe drive to cut deficits.
newsitem.headline: IMF warns of risks in Europe drive to cut deficits.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund warned Europe on Wednesday against persisting with its headlong drive to reduce budget deficits under the Maastricht Treaty if economic growth fails to pick up as expected.
"It is important to avoid aggravating a difficult situation through unduly procyclical (tight) fiscal policies," the IMF said in its semi-annual World Economic Outlook.
The Fund does expect European Union economic growth to pick up next year, to 2.5 percent, from 1.6 percent in 1996.

If that occurs, a number of nations, including France, should be able to cut their 1997 budget deficits in line with criteria set out in Maastricht and thus qualify for membership in European Monetary Union at its launch in 1999, it said.
But problems will crop up if growth remains weak -- a risk that the IMF made clear could not be ruled out.

In that case, the Fund signalled that it would prefer European nations to temporarily allow their budget deficits to increase in line with the weakness of their economies rather than to cut them to meet the tough Maastricht criteria.

"If recent economic weakness were to be prolonged, it may ... be necessary to allow fiscal policy to provide automatic stabilizers for activity, but only in those countries that are making convincing and adequate progress in reducing structural imbalances," the IMF said.
According to a chart in the World Economic Outlook, France and Germany, among others, would seem to qualify as countries making such progress.
The IMF made clear that in the medium term European countries need to put their public finances in order -- Maastricht or not.
"Progressive elimination of fiscal imbalances is necessary for an improvement in growth performance over the medium term," the IMF said.
And it linked Europe's high budget deficits to its excessive unemployment rates.

"As much as eight to nine percentage points of the EU's current unemployment rate of over 11 percent is widely considered to be structural in the sense that it is unlikely that it could be absorbed through cyclical recovery alone, without significant inflationary risks," the Fund said.
It backed widespread labor market reforms to tackle that.
